sources.title: MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research
sources.practitioner: Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc, Robert Zubek
sources.method: Mechanics-dynamics-aesthetics tuning loop; eight aesthetic targets as a compass; designers work M->D->A, players feel A->D->M.
sources.limitations: Full 5-page PDF read by the Grok design seat. 2004 workshop paper; later critiques not surveyed. Not a formula for fun and says so. Says nothing about production scheduling.

sources.title: Game Design Workshop, 5th Edition - playcentric excerpt
sources.method: Playcentric design: player experience goals written as felt situations, prototype the core immediately in the cheapest medium, playtest against the goals, iterate before production.
sources.limitations: Author-posted excerpt (2024-04-18) read; the full 5th edition was not read cover to cover. Physical prototypes under-serve real-time feel (see S06). Friend playtests bias results (Fulton, in S08).

sources.title: The Art of Game Design: A Book of Lenses (studio hub)
sources.method: Lenses: question sets used as diagnostics when a prototype feels wrong; not a checklist and not a pipeline.
sources.limitations: Official studio page fetched; book text not read cover to cover. Deck and app are untested tools. Using all lenses as a checklist is a misuse the method itself warns against.

sources.title: GDC 2012: Sid Meier on interesting decisions
sources.practitioner: Sid Meier (Firaxis); write-up by Leigh Alexander
sources.method: Decision tests: always-A and random-pick failures; tradeoffs, situational, persistent, play-style expressive; enough information; acknowledge every choice; cut systems that stay uninteresting.
sources.limitations: Contemporary write-up read; the GDC video was not frame-reviewed. Meier states rhythm and some puzzle games are a weaker fit. Civilization-heavy examples.

sources.title: A Theory of Fun for Game Design - author page and 2003 slides
sources.method: Fun as pattern learning; a loop dies once its pattern is mastered; long-lived games refresh the possibility space.
sources.limitations: Author page and hosted 2003 slides read; the book was not read cover to cover. Weak on fellowship, atmosphere and submission aesthetics. Games-are-not-stories claim is incomplete for presence-driven games.

sources.title: Game Feel: A Game Designer's Guide to Virtual Sensation
sources.method: Game feel = real-time control of a virtual object in a consistent spatial simulation plus polish; input latency and response metrics matter.
sources.limitations: Publisher pages and Library of Congress table of contents only; book body not read. Does not apply cleanly to turn-based, menu-driven or non-spatial games. 2008 input-hardware examples.

sources.title: The Door Problem
sources.method: Every interactable gets its full question list (open, lock, signal, pathing, unloading, audio, QA) and a role map before implementation.
sources.limitations: Live blog URL returned a stub; Wayback 2023-10-23 and the Kotaku reprint (author-permitted) were used. Essay is an analogy, not a complete spec standard. Large-studio role map does not transfer 1:1 to solo.

sources.title: Conversations From GDC Europe: Harvey Smith on systemic level design
sources.practitioner: Harvey Smith (Ion Storm); Bill Fulton (Microsoft User-Testing Group) in the same piece; interview by John McLean-Foreman
sources.method: Class-to-class rules over one-off triggers; second-order consequences; reward the goal not the method; Fulton: recruited strangers and research hygiene beat designer-observed friend tests.
sources.limitations: 2002 interview read. Deus Ex-era examples. Original GDC slides not recovered first-party. Production and QA cost of systemic design not quantified.

sources.title: Would the Real Emergent Gameplay Please Stand Up? (GDC 2004)
sources.method: Emergence rises when mechanics are connected through general stimuli (fire, noise) rather than hard-coded object pairs.
sources.limitations: GDC Vault listing and an unofficial 2017 slide-plus-audio reconstruction; not frame-reviewed. Randy Smith's separate object-oriented level design essay was not found at a stable URL.

sources.title: An Approach to Holistic Level Design (GDC 2017)
sources.method: Holistic level design: gameplay, presentation and story designed as one object; architecture-school thinking.
sources.limitations: Talk description and transcript snippets only; not frame-reviewed. Lee flags a 3D action-adventure and immersive-sim bias. Not a 2D, puzzle or management-game process.

sources.title: The Level Design Book - How to make a level

canonicalSteps.title: Environment Setup
canonicalSteps.reason: The bootloader still detects project mode, validates the runtime and persists state. For a game it additionally records which prototype media are available now (paper, tabletop, spreadsheet, greybox, sprite editor, DCC, engine), pins versions of any tool that is already chosen, and records the playtest capture path. An engine is not required to pass Step 0; unknown stays unknown.
inputs: Installed tools inventory (DCC, engine, sprite or audio editors, capture tools)

questions.prompt: Which prototype media can you use now without installing anything new (paper, cards, spreadsheet, text, greybox, sprite editor, DCC, engine)?
For every tool already chosen, what exact version is pinned (engine, official sample, DCC, IDE, middleware)? Write 'not chosen' where nothing is chosen.
How will playtests be captured (screen recording, notes template, input logs, photos of a tabletop)?
Which input devices and accessibility settings can you actually test with on this machine?

activities: Detect project mode and run the standard doctor
Record prototype media availability instead of forcing an engine install
Pin engine + sample + DCC + IDE versions together when any is chosen (marketplace listings and launcher caches can disagree)
Create the playtest log location and capture template
Record which official sample projects open cleanly, if an engine is pinned
outputs: Project baseline with a game section: prototype media, pinned versions, capture path
Empty playtest log with the evidence-grade vocabulary (transcript-only, sampled, exact)
reviewCriteria: Baseline names the prototype medium available now
Every pinned tool has an exact version or an explicit 'not chosen'
No engine was installed or chosen just to satisfy the doctor
revisionRules: Changing a pinned version re-opens technical.version-pins and any engine-validation phase that cited the old version
Adding a prototype medium never invalidates existing documents; removing one flags phases that depended on it

canonicalSteps.title: Ideation
canonicalSteps.reason: Step 1's product discovery (who, problem, outcome, evidence, Value Equation) stays. For a game the locked object is a set of player experience goals written as felt situations, an intended aesthetic mix, the core verb and the interesting decision, plus the assumptions that would kill the game. Features remain hypotheses about how to cause those situations. Independent idea packs and synthesis attach here when more than one contributor ideates.
inputs: Idea packs (one per contributor, or one solo pack)
Market and reference research (existing deep-research skill)

questions.prompt: Who plays, for how long per session, in what setting, and on what class of device? Describe people and situations, not an engine or platform.
Describe the intended player experiences as situations a playtest could confirm or challenge. Use only as many as the concept needs.
Which MDA aesthetics, if useful, describe the intended experience? Explain their priorities without forcing a quota.
What is the core verb the player performs, and what interesting decision surrounds it?
Which assumptions would kill the game if false (input latency tolerance, reading load, session length, a multiplayer requirement, a hardware class)?
Is the first thing to prove a decision, a feel, a story beat, a social space, or something else? Name one.

activities: Run the standard discovery interview with the game questions inlined
Record the experience-goal sheet as a living one-pager
Choose one primary evaluation method per prototype (decisions, feel, pattern mastery, verbs, presence) and keep the others as lenses
If several contributors exist, collect independent idea packs before any synthesis
Write MASTER_PRD with the game section: goals, aesthetic mix, verb, decision, kill-assumptions, hold list
outputs: Idea pack artifacts (one per contributor) and, when more than one, a synthesis record
reviewCriteria: A reviewer who has not seen a feature list can describe the intended session from the goals alone
Every goal is a situation a playtest could fail
The primary proof is named and matches the goals (a feel proof for a turn-based card game is a mismatch)
Kill-assumptions are stated, not hidden in features
revisionRules: A failed playtest changes the prototype, not the goal, unless the creator explicitly revises the goal and records why
Editing an idea pack re-opens any synthesis that selected it (dependency invalidation)
Adding a contributor adds a pack; it never rewrites existing packs

canonicalSteps.title: Offer Architecture
canonicalSteps.reason: Runs only when the creator answers that the game is monetized or platform economics matter (paid once, free-to-play, live service, DLC, cosmetics, subscriptions, platform fees, sponsorship). A store submission fee alone is not an offer. When it runs, provenance of sold assets becomes a shipping constraint. 'Not decided yet' keeps this step deferred with a reason and a revisit condition.
inputs: Distribution target class (PC storefront, console, mobile, web, physical) once known
Company operating map (Atlas 12) for finance and legal owners

questions.prompt: How does this game make money, if at all: none, paid once, optional extras, subscription, live economy, sponsored, other? 'Undecided' is allowed and defers this step with a revisit date.
Is this a completable work or an ongoing service with seasons or events? If ongoing, what retention loop hypothesis justifies it?
Which assets, characters, music or packs would be sold separately, and what license or provenance record does each need?
Which platform fees, revenue shares, certification costs or age-rating costs apply to the chosen distribution class?

activities: Run the standard offer architecture only for the chosen model
Record explicit 'no live ops' or a retention loop hypothesis
Attach provenance and license requirements to every sold asset family
Route pricing to the finance owner and terms to the legal owner recorded in the company operating map
outputs: Offer and positioning brief with the monetization model
reviewCriteria: The chosen model is a creator answer, not a template default
Live-ops work is justified by a retention hypothesis or explicitly excluded
Every sold asset has a license path
revisionRules: Changing the monetization model re-opens technical.monetization-entitlements and production.company-functions
Adding a sold asset family requires a provenance entry before its PRD can be approved

canonicalSteps.title: Architecture
canonicalSteps.reason: C4, ADRs, quality attributes and trust boundaries stay. Game architecture additionally names the interaction model (authored beats, systemic possibility space, or hybrid), the simulation tick and authority model, the asset master store, the save model and, if the product requires it, online services. Engine and platform choice is an ADR with an exit criterion here, or stays open with a bounded bake-off experiment. Choosing an art mode (3D, 2D sprite, vector, text, audio-only, abstract, hybrid) is an architecture decision, not an assumption.

questions.prompt: Is the game authored (scripted beats), systemic (connected rules producing second-order play), or a hybrid? Give one example of a class-to-class rule if systemic.
Which art mode does the product need: 3D, 2D sprite, vector, text, audio-first, abstract, or a mix? Why does the experience need that mode?
Is an engine or framework already locked by the product or team? If not, what bounded experiment will decide it and what is the exit criterion?
Where does simulation truth live (single local process, host, dedicated server, turn server, none)? Is there real-time control of a body or object?
What must persist between sessions, what must never persist, and how are old saves migrated?
Multiplayer or online services: none, local, asynchronous, online. If online, which authority and cheat surfaces exist?

activities: Write the interaction-model ADR (systems versus set pieces)
Write the art-mode ADR with the pipeline it implies (a text game has no mesh pipeline)
Write the engine ADR or a bake-off plan with exit criteria; pin versions when locked
Name the asset master store (DCC files, engine-native, sprite sheets, audio sources) and the interchange format
Scope online and save models; mark multiplayer not-applicable with a reason when the answer is none
outputs: ARCHITECTURE.md with interaction model, art mode, engine ADR or bake-off plan, simulation authority, save model, online scope
Stack profile with pinned versions or explicit unknowns
reviewCriteria: The interaction model is chosen with an example, not a label
The art mode follows the experience goals and names the pipeline it implies
Engine choice has an ADR or a bake-off with an exit criterion; no brand preference without one
Multiplayer and save scope are answered, not defaulted
revisionRules: Changing the art mode re-opens every characters, environments and interface phase that assumed the old mode
Changing the engine re-opens technical.version-pins, technical.interchange-contract and every engine-validation phase
Changing the interaction model re-opens systems.class-to-class-rules and levels.solution-graph

canonicalSteps.title: UX Design
canonicalSteps.reason: Experience goals, journeys, information architecture and Design DNA stay. For a game the journey must include the first session, the fail state and its recovery, optional content and the ending. Readability is treated as a perception problem (contrast, silhouette, focus, consistent mapping, never colour alone) before it is a visual-identity problem. Direction studies are allowed as constraints; final asset production waits for proofs.

questions.prompt: Walk the first ten minutes: what does the player learn, by doing what, without a text dump?
How does the player fail, know they failed, and recover? Where is 'stuck' and 'lost' handled?
At the real play camera or view, how does the player tell interactable from decorative, danger from safe, path from wall, and focus from background?
Diegetic, minimal, or full HUD? What must never be hidden behind an option?
What are the visual, audio and haptic acknowledgements for the core verb and for every decision?

activities: Run the standard UX design with game journeys added (first session, fail, recovery, optional, ending)
Produce direction studies (palette, silhouette language, reference board) as constraints, not final art
Define the readability test at play scale
Scope accessibility questions alongside experience goals (input, timing, reading load)
outputs: DESIGN.md direction studies and readability rules
reviewCriteria: Journeys cover first session, fail, recovery, optional content and ending

revisionRules: Changing an experience goal re-opens the journeys that served it
Changing the art mode re-opens direction studies

canonicalSteps.title: Flow Tree
canonicalSteps.reason: The screen inventory, transitions and zero-omission proof stay and are necessary but insufficient. Games add a space inventory (rooms, routes, fail-forward paths), a verb inventory (what the player can do where), a door or interactable inventory, and a contact-state inventory for controlled bodies (idle, start, stop, turn, jump, land, interact, hit, fail). Puzzle games may be nearly all verbs and no space; open worlds invert that.

questions.prompt: List every space or board the player occupies, its entrances, exits and fail-forward routes. Write 'no spaces' for menu, text or board games and describe scenes instead.
List every player verb and the first place it is taught.
List every interactable class (doors, switches, pickups, NPC talk) that needs a door-problem sheet.
If the player controls a body or object in real time, list its locomotion and interaction states. Otherwise write 'no controlled body' and why.
For every fail state, which screen or space does the player land in, and how do they get back?

activities: Build the standard screen inventory and transitions
Add the space, verb, interactable and contact-state inventories with traceability to experience goals
Prove every verb has a first-teach location and every fail state has a recovery path
Emit the machine-readable flow tree with the game inventories
outputs: Flow tree with screens, spaces, verbs, interactables and contact states
Traceability matrix: goal -> verb -> first-teach space -> recovery
reviewCriteria: Every verb has a first-teach location
Every fail state has a recovery
Every interactable class is listed for a door-problem sheet
Contact states exist only when a controlled body exists
revisionRules: Adding a verb adds a first-teach location and re-opens levels.teaching-fairness

canonicalSteps.title: Wireframe Prototypes
canonicalSteps.reason: Per-flow prototype PRDs stay (Track A or B). For a game the first prototypes are the cheapest medium that can fail the experience goals: paper or cards for decisions, a greybox with real input latency for feel, beat boards for story, a chat room or tabletop for social play, a blockout for space. Block meshes, greybox levels, a dummy mannequin and temporary audio events are legitimate prototype artifacts. A vertical slice is a later prototype, not the first.

questions.prompt: Which medium proves the primary uncertainty most cheaply, and why is anything more expensive unnecessary right now?
What observable behaviour in a playtest means the prototype passed (players hesitate productively, testers control the object untutored, a stranger finds the exit)?
What is deliberately left out of this prototype, and which later document owns it?
Who outside the team will play it, and how will the session be recorded?

activities: Write one prototype PRD per proof (decision, feel, story, social, space) rather than per screen when that is the truer unit
Specify greybox, block mesh, dummy body, placeholder audio and temp UI as acceptable fidelity
Plan the playtest protocol for each prototype and its evidence grade
Run /prd-json --mode prototype afterwards as usual
outputs: Per-flow or per-proof prototype PRDs under docs/prds/flows/
reviewCriteria: Each prototype names the uncertainty it kills and the cheapest medium that can kill it
Success is an observable behaviour, not a feeling reported by the designer
No hero art, final score or content volume is required to run the prototype
revisionRules: A prototype that fails changes the prototype or the mechanic; changing a goal instead is a recorded creator decision
A new primary proof adds a prototype PRD rather than expanding an existing one

canonicalSteps.title: Design System
canonicalSteps.reason: Tokens, component styling and theming stay for menus and HUD. Games add gameplay-readability tokens (interactable, path, danger, focus, ally, enemy) and budget tokens that become acceptance numbers: triangle and texel budgets per asset class, material counts, atlas sizes, pixels per unit and palette limits for 2D, animation timing bands, audio loudness targets. canonicalSteps.reason: The full state catalogue with recovery, announcements and focus stays for UI.
