Is any live editor bridge enabled, by whom, on which isolated copy, with what rollback?

atlasSteps.notes: Maps to canonical Step 14. Atlas never installs an editor bridge, runs game tools or publishes from this path.

atlasSteps.title: Readiness and handoff
atlasSteps.purpose: Review the connected plan, measurement requirements and outstanding setup: goal events, decision histograms, performance traces on the target hardware class, accessibility usage, provenance manifest, and every unverified property stated honestly.

questions.prompt: Does every experience goal have an event that shows it happened?
Which performance and stability traces are collected on the target hardware class?
Which properties are still unverified at handoff (collision, LOD, frame rate, multiplayer, packaging)?

atlasSteps.notes: Maps to canonical Step 15. Readiness reports state prepared plans separately from actual external results.

workflows.title: Discovery: player experience, verb, proof and idea packs
workflows.purpose: Lock what the game must make a player feel, the verb and decision that cause it, the assumptions that could kill it, and the cheapest first experiment. Holds the reserved creator profile and independent idea-pack documents.
workflows.applicability: Every game. The profile is answered once per project and revised when facts change. One idea pack per contributor; a solo creator writes one pack (or several alternatives) and may synthesize them alone. No engine, genre, platform, multiplayer or monetization answer is assumed; unknown answers stay unknown with a revisit condition.

phases.title: Creator profile
inputs: Whatever the creator already knows about the game, including nothing

questions.prompt: Are you working solo for now, or with contributors who will write their own idea packs? This can change later.
Which facts are already fixed by the product or the people (existing engine, existing IP, existing assets, a platform you must ship on, a team you already have)? Write 'none' where nothing is fixed.

Which of these are genuinely undecided right now: engine, art mode, genre, platform, multiplayer, monetization, deadline? Undecided is a valid answer and keeps the related work unresolved rather than skipped.
Which art modes are you open to (3D, 2D sprite, vector, text, audio-first, abstract, mixed)? Do not pick yet unless the product already did.
How many hours per week can you and any contributors realistically spend, and which skills do you hold yourself (design, code, art, audio, writing, production)?
How will you record playtests and experiments so results can be cited later (notes template, recordings, photos)?

activities: Answer once, revise when facts change
Convert 'fixed' facts into architecture inputs and 'undecided' facts into open questions with revisit conditions
Record capacity so later appetites are honest
outputs: Creator profile document (setup preference, not the game specification)
reviewCriteria: Fixed versus undecided is explicit for engine, art mode, genre, platform, multiplayer, monetization and deadline
No undecided item was turned into a default
revisionRules: Changing a fixed fact (for example the engine is now locked) re-opens technical.engine-platform-decision and any phase that cited the old answer
Switching creator mode never deletes idea packs; it only changes whether synthesis needs selected contributors
phases.evidenceRequired: None beyond the answers. This document is a setup preference. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Independent idea pack
inputs: Any references the contributor personally chose

questions.prompt: In one paragraph, what is the game and what should a player feel in one session?
Describe the player experiences this concept should create and how a playtest could challenge them.
Which MDA aesthetics, if useful, describe this concept, and how are they prioritized?
What does the player do, over and over, and what decision surrounds it?
What must be proved first: a decision, a feel, a story beat, a social space, a space to explore, something else?
What is the cheapest experiment that could show the primary proof fails (cards, spoken rules, spreadsheet, greybox, beat board, chat room)?
Which assumptions would kill this idea if false?
Which existing games, works or references shaped this, and what specifically was borrowed or rejected?
Anything you expect other contributors to disagree with, and why you hold your position?

activities: Write the pack without reading other contributors' packs
Keep the pack to what one person actually believes; do not union features from other games
Name the contributor in the document's contributor field (required for approval)
outputs: One idea-pack document per contributor, workspace-visible and independently authored
reviewCriteria: Goals are situations, not features
The primary proof matches the goals
A contributor is named
The pack was not edited to match another pack before synthesis
revisionRules: Editing a pack after a synthesis selected it invalidates that synthesis review through artifact revision propagation
A contributor may add a second pack as an alternative instead of overwriting the first
phases.evidenceRequired: None required for a draft. Approval requires a non-empty contributor and every required answer. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Experience-goal sheet
inputs: Selected idea pack or synthesis record

questions.prompt: Write the selected experience goals as situations, each with observable behavior that would show whether it held or failed.
Which evaluation method is primary for this game: interesting decisions, pattern mastery, game feel, verbs and scenes, or presence? Which stay as diagnostic lenses?
Who is allowed to change a goal after the first playtest, and how is the change recorded?
Session length, setting, interruption tolerance and device class, in plain language.

activities: Merge from the selected pack or synthesis; do not average dissent into mush
Attach the observable behaviour per goal
Name the primary method and the owner of goal changes
reviewCriteria: A reader who has not seen a feature list can describe the intended session
Each goal has a failing behaviour
One primary method is named
revisionRules: A failed playtest changes the prototype; a goal changes only by a recorded owner decision with a reason
Changing a goal re-opens primary-proof, kill-assumptions and every prototype that cited it
phases.evidenceRequired: None required beyond the sheet. Later phases cite this sheet; it is not itself proof. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Primary proof and prototype track

questions.prompt: Decision track (cards, spoken rules, spreadsheet, tabletop), feel track (greybox with realistic input latency), story track (beat boards, read-through), social track (chat room, tabletop with strangers), space track (blockout walk), or another? Pick one primary.

What tester behaviour means pass (players hesitate productively and can explain the tradeoff; testers control the object untutored and describe a body metaphor; a stranger finds the exit; a reader wants the next beat)?
If a second track is needed, which comes second and why not now?
Which prototype forms are explicitly unnecessary for this game (for example no 3D greybox for a text game, no paper prototype for a pure-feel game), and why?

activities: Choose one primary track from the uncertainty, not from habit
Write the pass signal as a behaviour
Record which forms are unnecessary so no one builds them
tools: Cards, paper, spreadsheet, text editor, greybox scene, sprite editor, chat room, tabletop - whichever the track needs
outputs: Primary-proof decision with pass signal and rejected forms
reviewCriteria: The track matches the uncertainty (no feel track for a turn-based card game)
The pass signal is observable
Unnecessary forms are named, not silently skipped
revisionRules: A new primary uncertainty adds a proof decision; it does not overwrite the record of the old one
phases.evidenceRequired: None required before the experiment. After the experiment, the playtest log entry and its evidence grade are attached in first-playtest. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Kill-assumption register

questions.prompt: List every assumption that would kill the game if false: input latency tolerance, reading load, session length, hardware class, a multiplayer requirement, a licensing dependency, the creator's own available hours.
For each assumption, the cheapest bounded experiment that could falsify it, and its cost in hours.
Which assumption is tested first and why (highest kill probability times lowest cost)?

activities: Write each assumption as a falsifiable statement
Attach a bounded experiment and cost to each
Order by kill probability over cost; the first experiment becomes first-playtest or a technical experiment
outputs: Kill-assumption register feeding MASTER_PRD and the quality workflow
reviewCriteria: Every assumption is falsifiable
Every assumption has a bounded experiment
Nothing in the register is a feature wish
revisionRules: A falsified assumption re-opens experience-goals or architecture, whichever it kills, by recorded decision
A new dependency (engine add-on, licensed music) adds an assumption
phases.evidenceRequired: Register only. Each experiment's outcome is recorded where it ran (first-playtest, technical.interchange-contract, quality.playtest-protocol) with its evidence grade. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: First evidence-focused playtest

questions.prompt: Who will play, or has played, how many, and who facilitates? Explain why these participants fit the uncertainty and what familiarity, recruitment or accessibility biases limit the evidence.
Exactly what was played (deck version, rules text, greybox build id, beat board revision)?
For each experience goal: held, failed, or not observable in this medium, with the behaviour seen.

Which facilitation method fits this test (silent observation, think-aloud, co-play or interview), and why? Record any actual intervention and whether it reveals a game issue, a test-design issue or an unresolved interpretation.
What evidence exists: notes only, photos, sampled recording, full recording? Where is it stored?
What changes in the prototype next, and which goal does the change serve?

activities: Prepare a test with a named uncertainty, participant rationale and facilitation method; external execution is a separate authorized activity
Log who, what, which goals held, and the evidence grade
Change the prototype, not the goal, unless the owner records a goal change
tools: Recording or notes per Step 0 capture path
outputs: Playtest plan, or an actual session log with evidence grade and next change
reviewCriteria: The playtest type is named (friends, strangers, platform, accessibility)
Goals are scored by behaviour, not by designer feeling
Evidence grade and storage location are recorded
revisionRules: Each new session appends an entry; earlier entries are never rewritten
A failed goal re-opens the prototype PRD; revise the goal itself only through a recorded creator decision with rationale
phases.evidenceRequired: An actual session must have happened: the log entry names players, medium, per-goal behaviour and the stored recording or notes. A planned session is recorded as planned, never as a result. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Production hold list

questions.prompt: Which work does the creator choose to hold until a named proof passes (content volume, hero art, full score, store page, live-ops design)? Each item needs the proof that releases it.
Which work may start now regardless (direction studies, tool pins, reference packs, accessibility scoping)?
For each held item, why is waiting cheaper than starting now? If starting now is cheaper (for example a solo artist who must practice), say so and release it.

activities: Write the hold list as creator choices with release conditions, not as a blanket freeze
Release anything whose early start is genuinely cheaper
Feed held items to feature breakdown as volume rows gated on proofs
outputs: Hold list with release conditions feeding MASTER_PRD and Step 10
reviewCriteria: Every held item has a release proof
No item is held by rule alone; each has a reason
Released early work is listed too
revisionRules: A passed proof releases its items in the same revision
Adding a held item requires a reason and a release proof
phases.evidenceRequired: None. The list is a plan; the release proofs are the evidence, recorded where those proofs ran. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Handoff into MASTER_PRD
inputs: Synthesis record when more than one pack exists

questions.prompt: Which discovery answers go into MASTER_PRD's game section (goals, aesthetic mix, verb, decision, primary proof, kill-assumptions, hold list) and which stay as working notes?
Which items remain undecided (engine, art mode, platform, multiplayer, monetization) with a revisit condition each?
Which company functions (finance, legal, marketing, community, operations) already have a decision or an owner from this discovery, and which are gaps?

activities: Write the MASTER_PRD game section from approved documents only
List undecided items with revisit conditions
Hand company-function links to Atlas 12
reviewCriteria: Every PRD statement traces to an approved document
Undecided items are listed, not defaulted
Company function gaps are named
revisionRules: Any upstream discovery revision invalidates this handoff until re-reviewed
phases.evidenceRequired: None beyond traceability to approved documents. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

workflows.title: Systems: interaction model, verbs, decisions, feel and economy
workflows.purpose: Turn the core verb into a proven loop: name the interaction model, inventory verbs and objects, test decisions for interest, prove feel where real-time control exists, plan progression or economy, write class-to-class rules for systemic play, and run the tuning loop with playtests.
workflows.applicability: Every game has at least a verb inventory and a decision audit. The feel track applies only when the player controls a body or object in real time. Class-to-class rules apply only to systemic or hybrid interaction models. Economy and progression apply when the game has resources or a mastery curve; a short authored work may mark them not-applicable with a reason.

phases.title: Interaction model decision

questions.prompt: Authored beats, systemic possibility space, or hybrid? Give one concrete example of how a moment is produced under the chosen model.
If systemic or hybrid: one class-to-class rule (any X plus any Y produces Z) and one second-order consequence you would accept without scripting it.
Which moments are deliberately special-case (a scripted exit, a set piece) even in a systemic game?
What production and QA cost does the chosen model imply, and does capacity from the creator profile cover it?

activities: Decide the model from the experience goals and the capacity
Write the architecture ADR text for Step 2
List special cases explicitly so they are not mistaken for missing systems
reviewCriteria: The model has a concrete example
Cost is compared to capacity
Special cases are listed
revisionRules: Changing the model re-opens class-to-class-rules, levels.solution-graph and narrative.story-structure
phases.evidenceRequired: Decision only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Verb and object inventory

questions.prompt: List every player verb, the object classes it acts on, and the resistance or cost each verb meets.
For each verb, where and how it is taught by doing, without a text dump.
Which verbs could be removed without losing an experience goal? Remove them or justify them.

activities: Enumerate verbs and object classes as a matrix
Attach the first-teach location per verb
Cut verbs that serve no goal
tools: Spreadsheet or table in the document
outputs: Verb-object matrix feeding the Step 4 flow tree
reviewCriteria: Every verb serves a goal
Every verb has a first-teach location
Object classes are classes, not one-off instances
revisionRules: Adding a verb re-opens decision-audit and levels.teaching-fairness
Removing a verb re-opens every level document that used it
phases.evidenceRequired: Inventory only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Decision audit

questions.prompt: List the decisions the player makes around the core verb, each with its tradeoff, what makes it situational, and how the game acknowledges it.
For each decision, the always-A test: could one option dominate? What evidence (playtest picks) do you have?
For each decision, could the pick be random without loss? What evidence?
Does the player have enough information to choose without paranoia, and how is it shown?
Which decisions stay uninteresting after tuning and are cut, and which test killed them?

activities: Run always-A and random-pick tests in the cheapest medium
Record pick counts from real testers
Cut or rewrite decisions that fail; do not schedule them for later polish
outputs: Decision audit table with pick evidence and cuts
reviewCriteria: In a small test no option is chosen unanimously or never without a situational reason
Every decision is acknowledged by the game
Cuts cite the test
revisionRules: New tester data that shows dominance re-opens the decision and any economy that depended on it
phases.evidenceRequired: Pick counts from real sessions (who, how many, which build) at a stated evidence grade. A predicted distribution is a plan, not a result. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Feel track (real-time control only)

questions.prompt: Does the player control a body or object in real time? If not, mark this phase not-applicable with that reason.
Input-to-motion latency target, acceleration and deceleration shape, camera behaviour, hit-stop and juice budget, and the body metaphor testers should describe.
Plan the same greybox at two latencies (for example 50 ms and 150 ms). What behaviour difference would prove feel matters for this game?
Which placeholder sounds (footstep, confirm, fail, hit) are part of the feel prototype?

activities: Build or specify a greybox with realistic input latency and placeholder audio
Select a suitable latency experiment and participants; distinguish creator self-tests from independent player evidence
Record whether testers can control the object untutored and describe the metaphor
tools: Greybox scene in any engine or framework
outputs: Feel specification with metrics and the latency experiment result
reviewCriteria: Not-applicable carries a reason
Metrics are numbers with a device class
The selected latency experiment has an execution receipt, or remains explicitly not executed with its participant limits recorded
revisionRules: Engine change re-opens the latency experiment
A camera or control change re-opens the feel metrics
phases.evidenceRequired: Recorded sessions at both latencies with tester behaviour and the input log or build id. Planned experiments are recorded as planned. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Progression and economy plan

questions.prompt: Does the game have progression (mastery curve, unlock tree, resource economy, narrative gating)? If not, mark not-applicable with a reason.
Which one is the player supposed to feel primarily: a learning curve, a decision tree that stays interesting, or an economy? Naming all three without a primary is the treadmill risk.
When the pattern is mastered, what refreshes the possibility space (permutation, competition, player-authored content, new layers of the same verb)? Or is the game meant to end?
Which spreadsheet or simulation model tests the curve before content is built?

activities: Name the primary progression feeling
Model the curve in a spreadsheet or simple simulation
Decide whether the game ends or refreshes
outputs: Progression and economy model with the primary feeling named
reviewCriteria: One primary progression feeling
The model exists before content volume
Refresh or ending is explicit
revisionRules: A changed decision audit re-opens the model
Adding a resource adds a model column
phases.evidenceRequired: Model runs (spreadsheet or script output) at the stated version, not projected numbers. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Class-to-class rules (systemic or hybrid only)

questions.prompt: Is the model systemic or hybrid? If authored, mark not-applicable with that reason.
Which general stimuli exist (fire, noise, water, money, light) and which object classes listen to each?
List the class-to-class rules in the form 'any X plus any Y produces Z'.
From the spark experiment, which emergent tricks are kept, which are blocked, which are taught?

activities: Write rules as class relations, not object pairs
Run the class-to-class spark experiment (two mechanics listening to one stimulus for ten minutes)
Decide keep, block or teach per emergent trick
outputs: Class-to-class rule table with keep/block/teach decisions
reviewCriteria: Rules reference classes
At least one second-order consequence was observed or the systems are still special-case
Keep/block/teach is recorded
revisionRules: A new object class must list which stimuli it listens to
A blocked trick re-opens levels.solution-graph if levels relied on it
phases.evidenceRequired: The spark experiment session: what two mechanics, what stimulus, what happened, recorded at a stated grade. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Tuning loop across mechanics, dynamics and aesthetics

questions.prompt: For the last change to a mechanic, which dynamics changed and which aesthetic moved? Record the cascade.
Which experience goals does the current build hold, by tester behaviour, and which fail?
Which single mechanic, rule or number changes next, and which goal it serves?
What result would mean the loop is proven and content volume may start?

activities: Change one lever, playtest, record the cascade
Score goals by behaviour each round
Stop when the stop condition holds and release held items
outputs: Tuning log with cascades and the proven-loop declaration
reviewCriteria: One lever per round
Goals scored by behaviour
The stop condition is stated before the round
revisionRules: A proven-loop declaration releases hold-list items; a later failed goal revokes it by recorded decision
phases.evidenceRequired: Per-round playtest entries with build id, testers and per-goal behaviour. The declaration cites the entries. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Systems instrumentation plan

questions.prompt: Which events expose each decision's pick distribution and each goal's occurrence in real play?
Which distributions would trigger a design revisit after release (for example one option above 80 percent)?
What is not collected, and how are players told?

activities: List decision and goal events for Step 15
Set revisit thresholds
Record privacy limits
outputs: Systems section of the instrumentation contract
reviewCriteria: Every audited decision has an event
Thresholds exist
Privacy limits are stated
revisionRules: A new decision adds an event
phases.evidenceRequired: Plan only; real distributions arrive after release. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

workflows.title: Narrative and world: load, rules, structure and delivery
workflows.purpose: Decide how much story the game carries and how it is delivered, write world rules as constraints for art and levels, structure beats as pressure on verbs, and test narrative with readers and players before cinematic or dialogue volume is produced.
workflows.applicability: Applies when the game has any narrative or a fictional world, including environmental storytelling with no text. A purely abstract game marks narrative-load as none and the remaining phases not-applicable with that reason. World rules still apply to any game with a setting, even without story.

phases.title: Narrative load decision

questions.prompt: None, environmental, quest or dialogue, cinematic, or authored-linear? Pick the primary and name secondary channels.
Which experience goal needs this load? A goal of presence or fellowship may need less text than a goal of narrative.
What does this load cost in writing, voice, scripting and rework when levels change, against capacity?
If the fiction were removed, what remains? If nothing, the loop is not yet proven and this is a stress test result, not a failure of the story.

activities: Choose the load from the goals and capacity
Run the fiction-removed stress test honestly
Feed the load into Step 2 and the level workflow (scripting weight)
reviewCriteria: Load matches a goal
Cost is compared to capacity
The stress test was answered
revisionRules: Changing the load re-opens levels.scripting-save-state and audio.core-verb-sounds (voice)
phases.evidenceRequired: Decision only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: World rules and constraints

questions.prompt: What are the world's readable rules: scale references (door, stair, human, vehicle), material language, technology level, what cannot exist?
Which rules constrain characters and environments (silhouette language, palette, era) and which are free?
Which rules constrain spaces (no elevators, water is deadly, doors are rare) and become door-problem inputs?
What is the smallest bible that serves art and levels now? What is deliberately not written yet?

activities: Write rules as constraints, not lore volume
Hand constraints to characters.identity-proportions and environments.world-rules-scale
Keep the bible small and dated
outputs: World-rules sheet with art and level constraints
reviewCriteria: Every rule is usable by art or levels
Scale references are concrete
Volume is deferred with a reason
revisionRules: Changing a rule re-opens every character and environment identity document that cited it
phases.evidenceRequired: Constraints only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Story structure as pressure on verbs

questions.prompt: List the beats (development, conflict, climax, resolution or the structure you chose) and, for each, which verb it pressures and how.
Where does the player's choice change the story, where does it not, and how is that honest to the player?
If the game is systemic, which beats are special-case and which emerge from rules?
How does the game end (or refresh), and which goal the ending serves?

activities: Write beats as pressure on verbs, not as cutscene volume
Mark authored versus emergent beats
Define the ending
reviewCriteria: Every beat pressures a verb
Agency is honest
The ending exists
revisionRules: A cut verb re-opens the beats that pressured it
A changed interaction model re-opens authored/emergent marks
phases.evidenceRequired: Beat sheet only; reader and player tests are recorded in narrative-playtest. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Delivery channels and scripting weight

questions.prompt: Which channels deliver story: environment, item text, dialogue, voice, cinematics, UI, music? What share does each carry?
For dialogue, quests or cinematics: which scripting, branching and localization cost does each channel add to levels and technical work?
When a level changes after story is placed, what gets rewritten? Which channels are cheapest to rework?
Voice acting: none, placeholder, final later? If final later, what is the placeholder rule?

activities: Assign shares per channel
Estimate scripting and rework cost per channel
Prefer cheap-to-rework channels while levels are unstable
reviewCriteria: Channel shares sum to the load
Rework risk is stated
Voice policy is explicit
revisionRules: Changing a channel share re-opens levels.scripting-save-state and audio.core-verb-sounds
phases.evidenceRequired: Plan only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Environmental storytelling plan

questions.prompt: Does the environment carry story? If the game has no spaces, mark not-applicable with that reason.
For each space, which beat or rule is shown by dressing, lighting or damage, with one sentence per space.
How will you test that players read the intended story from the space without text (playtest question list)?

activities: Map beats to spaces
Write the playtest question list
Hand dressing beats to environments.set-dressing-assembly
reviewCriteria: Each space has at most a few beats
The playtest questions are written before dressing starts
revisionRules: A removed space re-opens its beats
A changed beat re-opens the dressing plan
phases.evidenceRequired: Plan only; player reading is recorded in narrative-playtest. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Narrative read-through and player test

questions.prompt: Who read or heard the beats (strangers preferred), and which beats landed, confused or bored, by their words?
In a playable build, did players reconstruct the intended story? Ask them to retell it and record the gaps.
Did players feel the choices mattered where they were meant to, and not where they were not?
Which beat, channel or space changes next and why?

activities: Run a read-through and, when a build exists, a retell test
Score beats by tester words
Change beats or channels, not goals, unless the owner records a goal change
reviewCriteria: Testers are named by type
Retell gaps are recorded verbatim
Changes trace to gaps
revisionRules: Each session appends; earlier entries stand
phases.evidenceRequired: Actual sessions with tester type, build or draft version, retell text and stored notes or recording. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

workflows.title: Characters: identity to engine receipt
workflows.purpose: Take a playable being or creature from a locked identity through separate reference views, part sheets, geometry, comparison, UV, materials, rig, deformation, animation, contact states and engine validation. Each phase names its 2D, sprite, vector or text equivalent so the workflow does not assume a 3D mesh.
workflows.applicability: Applies to any character, creature, vehicle-as-character or avatar the player sees or controls. Games with no visible characters (text, abstract, pure UI) mark this workflow not-applicable with that reason. Background characters may skip phases according to their asset level from Step 10, each skip recorded with a reason. Art mode from the architecture decision picks the artifact names in each phase; 3D is never assumed.

phases.title: Identity and proportion lock

questions.prompt: Who is this character in play terms: what the player does with or against them, and which experience goal they serve?
Describe the silhouette in one sentence a stranger could draw from. What makes it distinct from every other character at play distance?
Proportion set in head-heights or a stated unit (for 2D: pixel height at native resolution and grid). Include scale references from the world rules.
Material or palette language: which surfaces, which colours or ramps, what is forbidden?
Which parts may change independently later (head, hair, outfit, weapon, cloth layers, palette swaps)?
Where did the design come from (own drawing, commissioned, generated, marketplace)? What license and provenance record exists?

activities: Write the identity package before any modelling or spriting
Run the lineup test: two reviewers pick this character from lookalikes using only the sheet
Record provenance in the sidecar draft
reviewCriteria: Two reviewers pass the lineup test
Proportions are in a stated unit with world scale references
Provenance is recorded, not 'we'll find out'
revisionRules: Changing proportions or silhouette re-opens every later character phase for this subject
A palette change re-opens texture-material-channels only
phases.evidenceRequired: Lineup test result: who reviewed, which lookalikes, pass or fail. Planned lineups are recorded as planned. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Separate reference views: front, back, side, three-quarter

questions.prompt: Which views exist as separate image files: front, back, left or right side, three-quarter, and optionally top? Each must be loadable alone as a camera background or sprite guide.
Does each view carry the same scale bar or head-height ticks and the same eye line?
Do the views agree with each other (feature heights line up across front and side)? Which discrepancies were found and fixed?
For sprite or vector work: the orthographic sheet and facing set (for example 4 or 8 directions) that replaces 3D views. Mark 3D views not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Produce each view as its own file, not a collage
Align feature heights across views with guide lines
For 2D, produce the facing set at native resolution
outputs: Separate view files (front, back, side, three-quarter) or the 2D facing sheet
reviewCriteria: Each view is a separate file with a scale reference
Feature heights agree across views
Views match the identity sheet in the lineup test
revisionRules: A changed view re-opens geometry-plan and multiview-comparison
phases.evidenceRequired: The files exist and a reviewer overlaid front and side at the eye line; note the discrepancies found. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Component, clothing, prop and material sheets

questions.prompt: Anatomy or structure sheet: which deformable regions exist (joints, jaw, cloth, tail, wheels) and which are rigid?
Component sheet: every named part (head, hair, torso, hands, feet, accessories) with its boundary and whether it is swappable.
Clothing sheet: layers in order, which layer covers which, forbidden intersections, and what is separate geometry versus painted.
Prop sheet: held or attached items with attachment points, sockets or pivot names, and which hand or slot.
Material sheet: per part the material or palette entry, roughness or shading style, emissive or special cases, and the target material or palette count.

activities: Produce one sheet per family; a single beauty render is not a sheet pack
Name every deformable part and every socket
Set the material or palette count against the Step 6 budget
tools: Spreadsheet for part and material lists
outputs: Anatomy, component, clothing, prop and material sheets
reviewCriteria: Every deformable part is named
Cloth layers and forbidden intersections are listed
Material or palette count is within budget or an exception is recorded
revisionRules: Adding a part re-opens geometry-plan, uv-layout, rig-plan
A material count change re-opens texture-material-channels
phases.evidenceRequired: The sheets use consistent part names. Record who reviewed them, what was checked and any independent review still needed. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Geometry, topology and LOD plan

questions.prompt: Triangle budget per LOD (or sprite size and frame count for 2D) with the hardware class it was set for.
Where must edge loops or density serve deformation (hips, shoulders, mouth corners, knees, elbows, hands, or the equivalent for this body plan)? For 2D: pivot placement and silhouette pixel rules.
Is there a high-poly detail donor and a retopologised runtime mesh, or a single mesh? For AI-generated or scanned sources: what decimation and cleanup plan?
Which surfaces are never visible at the play camera and will be removed (undersides, interior faces)?
LOD levels and the camera distance each must still read at; for 2D, mip or scaling policy.

activities: Write the plan before modelling
Set density by curvature then joints
Plan hidden-surface removal and decimation with before/after counts to record
outputs: Geometry plan with budgets, topology law, LOD policy
reviewCriteria: Budgets are numbers tied to a hardware class
Deformation zones are named for this body plan
Hidden-surface decisions are explicit
revisionRules: A budget change from Step 6 re-opens this plan
A new mutable part re-opens the LOD policy
phases.evidenceRequired: Plan only. Actual counts are recorded in multiview-comparison and engine-validation. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Multiview comparison of the built model against the references
inputs: Built block mesh or production mesh (or sprite set)

questions.prompt: For each view: was the model rendered orthographically at the same framing and overlaid on the reference view? Where did it deviate beyond the agreed pixel or percentage tolerance?
Actual vertex, triangle and object counts read from the tool per LOD, versus the plan.
Which test poses were checked (squat, reach, look-up, sit, grip, or this body plan's equivalents) and which regions pinched or tore?
Accept, fix and re-compare, or return to geometry-plan?

activities: Render orthographic stills at identical framing and lighting
Overlay against the separate view files and mark deviations
Read counts from the tool, never estimate
Pose the mesh in test poses before rigging
tools: DCC orthographic camera or sprite overlay
outputs: Comparison contact sheet with counts and deviations
reviewCriteria: Overlays exist for every view
Counts are tool-read
Deviations are within tolerance or a fix is scheduled
revisionRules: A failed comparison re-opens geometry-plan or view-sheets, whichever was wrong
A changed reference view invalidates the comparison
phases.evidenceRequired: The contact sheet images and the tool-read counts. On-screen stats are acceptable evidence; remembered numbers are not. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: UV layout (or atlas and pivot layout for 2D)

questions.prompt: Where are the seams, and why there (hidden by clothing, under arms, along hard edges)?
Measured texel density per region versus the target; which regions are intentionally denser (face, hands) and which sparser?
Atlas, UDIM tiles, or trim sheets? If UDIM, how will export split tiles for the engine? Edge padding per texture size?
For sprites: atlas packing, pivot per frame, filtering (nearest or linear), and palette lock. Mark UV items not-applicable with that reason.
Is geometry stable enough to unwrap? Which parts are expected to change and will need remapping?

activities: Unwrap when geometry is mostly stable
Check distortion with a test image
Measure density and record it
Set padding by texture size
tools: DCC UV editor or sprite atlas packer
outputs: UV layout with density measurements and padding, or the sprite atlas and pivot document
reviewCriteria: No unintended overlaps
Density within the agreed tolerance of the target
Padding matches texture size
UDIM export plan exists if used
revisionRules: Geometry edits after unwrap require remapping and re-review
A texel target change re-opens the layout
phases.evidenceRequired: Checker-image screenshot and the measured density numbers. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Textures and material channels

questions.prompt: Per material: which channels exist (base colour, normal, roughness, metallic, occlusion, emissive, alpha; or palette and ramp for 2D), which are baked from a high-poly, painted, generated seamless, or photographed?
Which textures are sRGB and which are linear or non-colour data? Packed channel layout if packed?
For baked channels: bake resolution, cage or ray distance, and which high-poly source. Are node-based colour corrections baked before export (node graphs do not travel)?
Texture sizes per platform tier and the material count versus budget.
Source and license per texture (photo, painted, generated with which tool and prompt, purchased pack)?

activities: Bake or paint channels per the contract
Document colour space and packing
Bake corrections into textures before export
Record provenance per texture in the sidecar
tools: DCC texture and bake tools, painting tool, or sprite palette tool
outputs: Texture set with channel manifest, colour spaces, sizes and provenance
reviewCriteria: Every listed channel exists as a file
Colour spaces are documented
No engine-unsupported node remains at export
Provenance is complete
revisionRules: A material count change re-opens the manifest
A changed interchange format re-opens packing and export settings
phases.evidenceRequired: The channel files and a rendered material preview at the intended lighting; bake logs where the tool provides them. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Rig plan: bind skeleton and control rig

questions.prompt: Shared engine skeleton, retargeted custom, or fully custom? Which retarget cost experiment justified it? For 2D: bones, mesh warp, frame swap, or none.
Bind or deform hierarchy versus control hierarchy: what goes in each, and how are they kept separate?
Rigging-input inspection: naming, joint orientation, symmetry, scale, whether the mesh can bend where the anatomy sheet says it must.
Is facial rigging a separate task from body rigging? Which one, if either, is in scope for this asset level?
Bone influence cap for the interchange format (commonly 4 or 8) and how weights will be limited.
Which auto-rig or auto-pose tools are used, and what are their stated limits (humanoid only, no fingers or face)?

activities: Inspect the mesh as a rigging input before rigging
Decide skeleton policy from the retarget experiment
Separate deform and control hierarchies
Scope face versus body
tools: DCC rigging tools, engine retarget tools, or 2D skeletal tool
outputs: Rig plan with skeleton policy, hierarchy split, influence cap, inspection findings
reviewCriteria: Inspection findings are recorded before rigging
Hierarchies are separated
Influence cap matches the interchange contract
Tool limits are recorded
revisionRules: A skeleton policy change re-opens deformation-validation, locomotion-action-animation and engine-validation
A mesh change re-opens the inspection
phases.evidenceRequired: Inspection notes with the actual findings; the retarget experiment result (hours to first non-sliding walk on dummy versus custom) if run. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Deformation validation

questions.prompt: Which test poses were run (squat, reach, look-up, sit, grip, twist, or the body plan's set) and which regions collapsed, candy-wrapped, pinched or interpenetrated?
Which corrective shapes, helper joints or weight fixes were applied, and which problems were accepted at this asset level?
Do cloth layers and props follow the body without intersection in the test poses?
For 2D bones or mesh warp: which stretch limits and swap sets were checked? For frame swap: not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Run the pose set in the DCC or 2D tool
Fix or accept per region with a reason
Capture stills per pose
outputs: Deformation report with per-pose stills and accepted defects
reviewCriteria: Every pose has a still
Accepted defects carry a reason and asset level
Cloth and props were posed too
revisionRules: A mesh or weight change re-runs the pose set
A new pose in the contact set adds a test pose
phases.evidenceRequired: Per-pose stills from the tool. A written 'looks fine' is not evidence. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Locomotion and action animation

questions.prompt: Which clips exist: idle, start, stop, walk and run at the project's speed bands, pivot or turn-in-place, jump, land, fall, interactions (pickup, door, use, fire), hit-react, fail states (slip, blocked, down)? Adapt for non-biped body plans or 2D frame sets.
Hand-keyed, motion captured, purchased, generated, or engine warping (distance match, stride and orientation warp) on fewer clips? What license applies to purchased or generated clips?
Frame counts or durations against the timing tokens (windup, hit-stop, recovery).
One action per track or clip for export; which properties animate (transforms, bones, shape keys) and which do not travel through the interchange format?

activities: Author or acquire the clip set
Match timing tokens
Prepare export per the interchange rules
Record clip provenance
tools: DCC animation tools, mocap or clip library, sprite frame editor
outputs: Clip set with timing, source and export manifest
reviewCriteria: The set covers the contact-state inventory
Timing matches tokens or an exception is recorded
Provenance per clip exists
revisionRules: A new verb adds clips
A timing token change re-opens the set
phases.evidenceRequired: Playblasts or frame strips per clip and the export manifest. Playblast quality is not engine validation. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Contact and intermediate states
inputs: State spec body states from Step 7

questions.prompt: How are feet or contact points kept on ground at each speed band (foot IK, distance matching, frame-locked pivots for 2D)? What foot-slide tolerance is accepted?
For each pair of states that can follow each other (idle to run, run to jump, land to idle, any to hit-react), what plays in between and how long?
Which sockets, hitboxes or hurtboxes must meet weapons, props or UI anchors, per state?
What do slip, blocked, down and get-up look like, and how does the player know they can act again?
What happens to the pose and the face at LOD switches; can a facial rig fight a body LOD?

activities: Write the transition matrix
Define contact tolerances and hitboxes
Plan LOD and face behaviour at switches
tools: Engine animation graph or 2D state machine
outputs: Transition matrix, contact tolerances, hitbox and socket table
reviewCriteria: Every state pair that can occur has an intermediate
Tolerances are numbers
Fail and recovery are visible to the player
revisionRules: A new state from Step 7 adds a row and column
A changed speed band re-opens contact tolerances
phases.evidenceRequired: Matrix and tables; actual in-engine playback is proven in engine-validation. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Engine validation and receipt

questions.prompt: Import log: unknown materials, missing textures, bone count, vertex count after interchange splits, warnings. Zero unknown-material warnings?
Three-way comparison stills at the same pose: reference sheet, DCC render, engine render at the game's lighting path. Where do they differ?
Did the full contact set play at gameplay speeds in engine with feet within tolerance, sockets meeting props, no mesh explosion at LOD switch? Which states failed?
One performance sample on the target hardware class (or the closest available, stated honestly): frame time, animation thread cost, GPU memory for this asset alone and in a representative scene.
Was the provenance sidecar copied into the cooked or imported record, with license allowing the target stores?
What remains unverified (other platforms, multiplayer replication, final lighting)?

activities: Import into the pinned engine
Capture the three-way stills
Play the contact set and record failures
Take the performance sample with pinned quality settings
Attach the sidecar
outputs: Engine receipt for this character (import log, three-way stills, contact playback result, performance sample, sidecar copy)
reviewCriteria: Every receipt item exists as a file or log
Failures are listed with the state name
The hardware class of the sample is stated
Unverified items are listed
revisionRules: Engine version change re-runs the receipt
Any upstream character revision invalidates the receipt
phases.evidenceRequired: The receipt files themselves: import log, three-way stills, playback recording or frame captures, profiler sample, sidecar copy. A receipt produced by Atlas does not exist; Atlas only lists what must be attached. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

workflows.title: Environments: world rules to engine handoff
workflows.purpose: Build a playable space from readable world rules through decomposition, blockout, modular kit, hidden-surface culling, material and bake contracts, assembly order, lighting, collision, navigation, streaming and engine validation. 2D tile, vector, text-room and abstract-board equivalents are named per phase.
workflows.applicability: Applies to games with spaces, boards or settings the player perceives: 3D worlds, 2D tile maps, vector scenes, isometric boards, text-described rooms and audio-described navigable places. Games without a meaningful spatial or setting model mark the workflow not-applicable with a reason; audio-only or card-based presentation alone does not establish that. Background spaces may skip phases per asset level with a recorded reason.

phases.title: World rules and scale for this space
inputs: Play camera or view from Step 3

questions.prompt: What does this space do for play (teach, test, rest, reveal, connect) and which experience goal it serves?
Real-unit scale references present in the space (door, stair, human, vehicle; for 2D: tile size and character height in tiles). What is the play camera or view and its field of view?
Which world rules must be readable here (material language, what is climbable, what is deadly) and how are they shown without text?
Target traversal times or path lengths between key points, and why those numbers?

activities: Write the space brief
Fix scale references and camera before any geometry
Set traversal targets
outputs: Space brief with scale, camera, readable rules, traversal targets
reviewCriteria: Scale references are concrete
Camera or view is fixed
Traversal targets have reasons
revisionRules: A camera change re-opens blockout and hidden-surface-cull
A world-rule change re-opens readable rules
phases.evidenceRequired: Brief only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Decomposition map

questions.prompt: List every chunk of the space with a size class (anchor with known real size, volume, accessory) and a generation route (built by hand, kitbashed, image-to-3D high-poly, image-to-3D low-poly, primitive, cut from existing, tile set, hand-drawn). Every visible region of the concept belongs to exactly one chunk.
Which chunks are anchors with a real size written down before anything is generated or drawn?
For grouped generation of small props, the expected count per group, so drift (asked four, got three) is caught.
For tile maps or vector scenes: the tile or symbol inventory and which are unique versus repeated. Mark 3D routes not-applicable with that reason.
Per chunk: source and license (own, purchased, generated with which tool)?

activities: Annotate the concept into chunks
Assign size class and route per chunk
Record expected counts and provenance
outputs: Decomposition map (annotated image plus chunk table)
reviewCriteria: Every region belongs to one chunk
Anchors have real sizes
Expected group counts are written
revisionRules: A concept change re-opens the map
A new chunk needs a route and provenance
phases.evidenceRequired: The annotated image and the table. Generated outputs are checked against expected counts in modular-kit. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Blockout (or tile-map draft, or room graph for text)
inputs: Level intent if a level owns this space

questions.prompt: Greybox volumes in an engine or DCC, a 2D tile draft, a paper map, or a text room graph? Why is that the cheapest playable form for this game?
Can a tester traverse it with the real camera and controls (or read it, for text)? Which routes and sightlines were checked?
Measured traversal times or path lengths versus targets.
Did an outsider find the intended path without help? Where did they get lost?
Confirm no hero art or final materials were placed; what placeholder rule was used?

activities: Build the cheapest playable form
Test the selected traversal and camera hypothesis with suitable participants; record self-test versus independent-player limitations
Measure traversal and record wayfinding failures
tools: Engine or DCC greybox, tile editor, paper, or text
outputs: Blockout with traversal measurements and wayfinding notes
reviewCriteria: Traversal targets met or revised with a reason
The chosen traversal experiment has recorded evidence and participant limitations, or is explicitly not executed
No hero art present
revisionRules: A failed wayfinding test re-opens the blockout, not the art plan
A camera change re-runs the walk
phases.evidenceRequired: Recording or notes of the chosen traversal experiment, measurements where relevant, and who participated. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Modular kit and starter pack

questions.prompt: Which chunks become kit pieces on a grid with snapping (or tiles with edge rules), and which are unique?
Per asset: source, triangle count before and after cleanup (tool-read), texture channels present, atlas membership, UV state (raw, unwrapped, packed), material name, license.
Did generated groups deliver the expected count? Which drifted?
How are seams between modules handled (texel match, snap grid, tile edges) so there are no gaps or light leaks?

activities: Build or acquire pieces
Fill the manifest from tool-read counts
Check generated counts against expectations
Test module seams
reviewCriteria: Counts are tool-read
No shared-atlas asset keeps a raw generated UV
Seams tested
revisionRules: A budget change re-opens the manifest
A new chunk adds a row
phases.evidenceRequired: The manifest with tool-read counts and a seam test screenshot. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Hidden-surface cull and decimation pass

questions.prompt: Which assets exceed the large-asset threshold and get an explicit decision?
Per large asset: 'underside or backside removed' or 'kept because visible', with the method (knife, boolean, decimate ratio, tile trim) and before/after counts read from the tool.
After decimation, does each piece still read at its intended camera distance?
For 2D: which off-screen or always-covered tiles and frames were removed from atlases? Mark 3D items not-applicable with that reason.

activities: List large assets
Cut or decimate with recorded counts
Re-check silhouettes
outputs: Cull report with per-asset before/after counts
reviewCriteria: Every large asset has a decision
Counts are tool-read
Silhouettes still read
revisionRules: A camera change re-opens cull decisions
phases.evidenceRequired: Before/after stats captures per asset. The one frame-verified example in the corpus is a single rock going from 922 to 448 vertices; that number is not a target. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Material and bake contract

questions.prompt: Per material: baked channels (from which high-poly), generated seamless tiles, painted channels, bake resolution, colour space.
Which colour corrections live in node graphs and must be baked before export?
Atlas membership and padding per texture size; UDIM or trim usage and export splitting.
Which decimated assets need baked normals to read as detailed at player distance?
For 2D: palette lock, filtering choice, and atlas size. Mark bake items not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Write the per-material contract
Bake and verify outputs exist
Record provenance per texture
tools: DCC bake tools, painting tool, tile tool
outputs: Material and bake manifest with output files
reviewCriteria: Every listed output exists
Corrections are baked
Padding matches size
revisionRules: A material count change re-opens the manifest
A decimation change re-bakes normals
phases.evidenceRequired: Output files and one lit preview per material family. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Assembly order and set dressing

questions.prompt: Which known-size anchor is placed first, and why not the enclosing volume?
Order of volumes, then accessories last; one collection or layer per chunk so any chunk hides with one click.
Is the reference image placed in the scene at scale?
Which narrative or world beats does dressing show, per area, and what is deliberately left bare?
Which pieces are reused by cut and scale (for example stalactites from a rock) and which must be unique?

activities: Place the anchor first
Assemble volumes then accessories with per-chunk collections
Dress against the beat map
outputs: Assembly plan and dressed scene with per-chunk collections
reviewCriteria: The plan starts from a known-size chunk
Accessories are last
Every chunk can be hidden alone
revisionRules: A blockout change re-opens the assembly
A beat change re-opens dressing for that area
phases.evidenceRequired: Scene outliner or layer screenshot showing per-chunk collections and total object and triangle counts read from the tool. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Lighting for gameplay and mood

questions.prompt: Which lights serve gameplay (readable path, cover, depth, danger) and which serve mood?
Which lighting path does the engine use for this game (baked, dynamic, mixed; or 2D lights and shadows; or none)? Preview lights in a DCC are not the game's lighting.
Lightmap resolution or dynamic light count budget and the hardware class.
How will you test that players read path and danger from light alone?

activities: Plan lights by function first
Use the engine's lighting path for review
Plan the perception test
outputs: Lighting plan with function map and budget
reviewCriteria: Every light has a function
The path is the engine's
A perception test is planned
revisionRules: A readability token change re-opens the function map
phases.evidenceRequired: Engine screenshots at the game's lighting path; the perception test result is recorded in the quality workflow. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Collision, navigation and streaming
inputs: Technical spec streaming and collision policy

questions.prompt: Simplified hulls per piece or per chunk; which visual geometry is not collision; which verbs need precise collision (climb, vault)?
If agents or companions move: navigation volumes and a path for every intended route. If none, not-applicable with that reason.
Load units and their budgets; expected hitch when crossing a unit; what is always resident.
If the space holds puzzle or world state: explicit states, reset path and what a mid-state save restores.
For 2D: tile collision layers, one-way platforms, and chunk loading. Mark 3D items not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Author collision and navigation
Define load units and budgets
Test every intended route
reviewCriteria: Every intended route has a path
Collision matches verbs
Load units have budgets
revisionRules: A new verb re-opens collision
A new route re-opens navigation
phases.evidenceRequired: Route test results and, where streaming exists, a hitch measurement per unit crossing. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Engine handoff checklist and receipt

questions.prompt: Which materials must be recreated in the engine by hand, and were they, with import warnings listed?
Which systems are left to the engine (water, sky, weather, grass, cloth, floating objects) and what does each depend on?
License status of every non-AI dependency (engine add-ons, packs, fonts). Does any paid or restricted add-on contradict a 'free' or 'open' assumption?
Receipt items: traversal times in engine, nav and collision result, mid-state save and load, streaming hitch versus budget, lighting at the game's path, performance sample on the hardware class.
What has not been verified (collision on other platforms, target frame rate, packaging, multiplayer)?

activities: Import and recreate materials
Fill the licensing table
Attach receipt items
List unverified properties
outputs: Engine handoff checklist and environment receipt
reviewCriteria: Every dependency has a license status
Receipt items exist as files
Unverified list is honest
revisionRules: Engine version change re-runs the receipt
A new dependency adds a license row
phases.evidenceRequired: Receipt files: import log, engine screenshots, route and save test results, hitch and performance samples. A licensing table with sources. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

workflows.title: Levels and puzzles: intent to art-pass readiness
workflows.purpose: Design a level, encounter, puzzle or scene as a graph of verbs, states and spaces: intent, constraints, solution graph, door-problem sheets, layout, blockout playtest, teaching and fairness, recovery, scripting and save state, and the gate that allows an art pass.
workflows.applicability: Applies to any bounded play unit: a 3D level, a 2D stage, a puzzle, a card scenario, a text chapter, a board setup, a multiplayer map. Phases about spaces are marked not-applicable with a reason for spaceless units; the solution graph, door sheets, teaching, fairness and recovery apply to every unit. Combat-specific work applies only when combat exists.

phases.title: Level intent

questions.prompt: Which experience goal does this unit serve, and what should a player feel at its start, middle and end?
Which verbs are featured, which are introduced for the first time, which are combined for the first time?
Which narrative beat, if any, this unit carries.
What observable tester behaviour means this unit works?

activities: Write the intent in one page
Name featured and first-time verbs
Write the success behaviour
reviewCriteria: One goal, named
First-time verbs are explicit
Success is a behaviour
revisionRules: A cut verb re-opens intent
A goal change re-opens intent
phases.evidenceRequired: Intent only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Constraints inventory

questions.prompt: Which world rules constrain this unit (no elevators, water deadly, doors rare)?
Streaming, memory, agent count, physics object budget, and any multiplayer symmetry or spawn constraints.
Which accessibility scoping answers bind this unit (no forced timers, remappable input, no colour-only signal, motion limits)?
Does combat exist here? If yes, define the fight before mapping it (enemy classes, ranges, cover needs). If no, mark not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Collect constraints from world, technical and accessibility documents
Define combat if present
outputs: Constraints inventory with combat definition if any
reviewCriteria: Every constraint cites its source document
Combat is defined or excluded with a reason
revisionRules: A budget change re-opens technical constraints
A new accessibility answer re-opens the inventory
phases.evidenceRequired: Inventory only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Solution graph

questions.prompt: List the unit's states (locked, open, powered, discovered, solved, failed) and the transitions the player's verbs cause.
Which solutions are intended, which are emergent and accepted, which are blocked, which are taught?
The shortest path from entry to goal, and every optional branch with its reward.
Which states are unrecoverable without reset? Each needs a recovery plan in recovery-fail-states or a reason to keep it.

activities: Draw the state graph
Mark intended, emergent, blocked, taught
Find dead ends
outputs: Solution graph with critical path and dead-end list
reviewCriteria: Every state is reachable and leaves
Emergent solutions have a keep/block/teach mark
Dead ends are listed
revisionRules: A blocked class-to-class trick re-opens the graph
A new verb may add transitions
phases.evidenceRequired: Graph only; tester paths are recorded in blockout-playtest. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Door-problem sheets for every interactable

questions.prompt: For each interactable class in this unit: can it be used, by whom, when, how does the player know, what is locked or gated, how do enemies or companions treat it, what unloads behind it, what sound or animation plays, how is it tested?
Count the unanswered items per sheet. Those are hidden scope; who owns each?
Which role (design, art, audio, technical, quality) owns each answer for this project? A solo creator lists themself and the order they will answer.

activities: Fill one sheet per interactable class
Count unanswered items as scope
Map owners
reviewCriteria: Every interactable class has a sheet
Unanswered items are counted, not hidden
Owners exist
revisionRules: A new interactable class adds a sheet
An unanswered item that blocks implementation blocks the PRD
phases.evidenceRequired: The sheets. The first unanswered-item count on the most boring interactable is the experiment result to record. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Layout plan
inputs: Space brief if a space exists

questions.prompt: 2D plan, node map, board diagram, or scene list? Why this form for this unit?
Where are entry, goal, key states, optional branches, sightlines to the goal or its promise, and rest points?
Intended pacing curve (tension, release) along the critical path, in plain words.
If multiplayer: symmetry, spawn fairness, and spectator or downed-player views. If not, not-applicable with that reason.

activities: Draw the plan as communication
Place states and sightlines
Describe pacing
reviewCriteria: Every graph state has a place
Sightlines to the goal or its promise exist
Pacing is described
revisionRules: A graph change re-opens the plan
phases.evidenceRequired: Plan only. Evidence text must separate what was planned from what actually happened; the existence of this document proves nothing about the game.

phases.title: Blockout playtest of the unit
inputs: Environment blockout if a space exists

questions.prompt: Playable greybox, paper walk-through, card scenario, or text draft? Why is this the cheapest form that can fail the intent?
Who will play, or has played, how many, and which facilitation approach fits the question? Record the participant selection limits and any intervention.
Which paths did testers take versus the critical path? Where did they get lost, stuck, or bored, by their behaviour?
Did the intended feelings at start, middle and end appear in tester behaviour or words?
What changes in the layout or graph next, and why?

activities: Build the cheapest playable form
Run the chosen experiment with suitable participants and record the limits of any creator-only test
Record paths, stuck points and words
Change layout or graph, not intent, unless the owner records an intent change
tools: Engine greybox, paper, cards, or text
outputs: Blockout playtest entries with paths and stuck points
reviewCriteria: Tester type is named
Paths are recorded against the critical path
Changes trace to observations

workflows.title: Team: contributors, explicit synthesis, decision record and revision propagation
workflows.purpose: Let a solo creator or a small group ideate independently and converge explicitly: name contributors, synthesize selected idea packs with agreements, disagreements, alternatives, chosen direction and reasons, unresolved matters and next experiments, record decisions, and define how revisions propagate to dependent documents.
workflows.applicability: Every game. Solo creators may write several alternative packs and synthesize them alone; team mode adds creator-selected contributors with no fixed team size or timebox. Synthesis must select at least one same-project idea-pack revision; the helper records source revisions and dependencies. Imported references never bind to foreign or missing records.
